nodes.title: Cryptography fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Crypto is the math layer that makes the rest of security possible. Most exam questions test symmetric vs asymmetric, hashing vs encryption, when to use which, and how key management actually works in practice.

flashcards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Symmetric (AES-256, ChaCha20): one shared key, fast, used for bulk data. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): public/private key pair, slow, used to exchange a symmetric key or to sign. Real systems use both: asymmetric to negotiate, symmetric to encrypt the bulk traffic (this is how TLS works).

flashcards.front: What's the difference between hashing and encryption?
flashcards.back: Encryption is reversible — the holder of the key can recover the plaintext. Hashing is one-way — you cannot derive the input from the output. Hashes are for integrity (did the file change?) and password storage (compare hashes, never store plaintext). SHA-256 is the modern default; MD5 and SHA-1 are broken.

A signature is a hash of the message encrypted with the signer's private key. Anyone with the public key can verify (decrypt the signature, recompute the hash, check they match). This proves authenticity (the holder of the private key signed it) AND integrity (the message wasn't tampered with).

flashcards.front: Why use a key management service (KMS)?
flashcards.back: Raw key handling is hard to do safely — you have to rotate, audit, restrict, destroy. A KMS holds keys in hardware, exposes encrypt/decrypt APIs, logs every use, enforces who can use which key. Your application code never sees the actual key material. AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS all play this role.

pairs.stem: A security team discovers that financial audit records are being automatically purged after 18 months. Applicable regulations require a mandatory 7-year retention period for these records. Which data management requirement is being violated?
pairs.option: Retention policy compliance — records are being destroyed before the legally mandated retention period expires

pairs.stem: A risk assessment reveals that patching a legacy system to close a known vulnerability would cost $250,000, while the maximum expected loss from exploitation is only $40,000. The organization documents this gap and accepts the exposure. Which risk treatment option best describes this decision?
pairs.option: Risk acceptance — the mitigation cost exceeds the expected financial impact, making acceptance cost-effective

pairs.stem: Before imaging a server involved in a suspected insider data theft, a forensic investigator photographs the physical device, documents its current state, and records the name, timestamp, and signature of every person who subsequently handles the hardware. What forensic principle do these documentation steps collectively preserve?
pairs.option: Order of volatility — capturing the most transient evidence first ensures nothing is lost when the system is powered down

pairs.stem: A legacy payment service continues negotiating TLS 1.0 sessions because neither the client nor server has been updated to enforce a minimum protocol version. Which attack category is MOST directly enabled by sustained use of TLS 1.0 in this deployment?
pairs.option: Certificate revocation bypass — TLS 1.0 clients cannot check OCSP stapling responses to verify certificate validity

pairs.stem: A web application builds a SQL query by directly concatenating an unvalidated URL parameter into the query string. An attacker submits the value `1; DROP TABLE orders;--` as the parameter and successfully deletes the orders table. Which vulnerability class does this attack represent?
pairs.option: Insecure deserialization — the URL parameter value is converted into a harmful object by the application runtime

pairs.stem: A developer stores a SHA-256 hash of each configuration file on a tamper-evident logging server at deployment time. During an audit, a configuration file's computed hash does not match its stored baseline value. Which security property does this hash-comparison control primarily enforce?
pairs.option: Integrity — the hash comparison detects whether the file was modified after its baseline value was recorded

nodes.title: Identity and access management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.

pairs.stem: An organization's CISO is preparing a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) for a Tier-1 application. The team needs to set a value indicating how much data the business can afford to lose in a disaster, measured in time. Which metric represents this?
pairs.option: RPO — the maximum acceptable age of data at the moment of recovery

pairs.stem: An organization is implementing zero-trust network architecture. Which principle BEST captures the core idea that drives zero-trust design decisions?
pairs.option: All traffic inside the corporate network is trusted because the perimeter firewall has already filtered untrusted sources

pairs.stem: A network team is designing segmentation for a corporate environment that includes a guest WiFi, an employee LAN, a server VLAN, and a regulated PCI cardholder-data zone. Which approach BEST aligns with defense-in-depth principles?
pairs.option: Use a flat Layer-2 network with strong endpoint EDR coverage so any compromised host is immediately detected and isolated

pairs.stem: An organization needs to grant a contractor access to specific files in a corporate document store. The contractor needs read-only access for 90 days, after which access must end automatically. Which IAM control combination BEST satisfies the requirement with least friction?
pairs.option: Provision the account in a 'contractors' security group with read-only ACL on the relevant folder; set an account expiration date of 90 days in the directory service

pairs.stem: A user wants to send a confidential message to a colleague using asymmetric cryptography, ensuring that only the intended recipient can decrypt it. Which key does the sender use for the encryption operation?
pairs.option: The recipient's public key — only the recipient's corresponding private key can decrypt what this public key encrypts

pairs.stem: An organization classifies a dataset as 'Confidential — Customer Financial'. The data owner mandates encryption at rest, access logging, and a 7-year retention policy. After 7 years, what is the appropriate disposition?
pairs.option: Anonymize the data and retain it for analytics, since anonymization removes personal identifiers and regulatory scope

nodes.title: Incident response: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IR follows a documented lifecycle so a panicked 3am pager doesn't turn into 'what do we do now?'. The classic NIST flow is preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. Exam questions test which phase owns which action.

flashcards.front: NIST IR lifecycle — name the phases.
flashcards.back: (1) Preparation: playbooks, contact lists, hardened images. (2) Detection & Analysis: SIEM alerts, IDS, user reports. (3) Containment: short-term (isolate host) + long-term (block C2 domains). (4) Eradication: remove malware, close vuln. (5) Recovery: restore from clean backup, monitor for re-infection. (6) Lessons learned: post-mortem within 2 weeks, action items tracked.

Short-term: stop the bleed fast — pull the network cable, kill the user session, block the IP. May be reversible. Long-term: durable fix — patch the vuln, rotate creds, deploy IPS rule, sometimes rebuild from scratch. Don't skip short-term: every minute of attacker dwell time multiplies damage.

flashcards.front: Chain of custody — why does it matter?
flashcards.back: If the incident leads to prosecution, evidence must be admissible — every transfer, image, and access logged from acquisition to court. Drives required to be hashed (SHA-256) immediately, copies (not originals) used for analysis, originals stored in a tamper-evident bag with signatures. Skip this and the lawyer dismisses your case.

flashcards.front: What's a post-mortem (lessons learned) supposed to produce?
flashcards.back: Blameless write-up within 2 weeks: timeline, what worked, what didn't, action items with owners + due dates. The goal is process improvement, not punishment — if engineers fear blame they hide details and the next incident is worse. Track action items in your normal sprint board, not in a doc nobody reopens.

pairs.stem: A security engineer is reviewing an application's authentication flow. The application stores user passwords using SHA-256 with a per-user salt. What is the MOST significant weakness in this approach for protecting passwords against modern offline attacks?
pairs.option: SHA-256 is a fast, general-purpose hash; modern GPUs compute billions of guesses per second, making brute-force feasible against weak passwords

pairs.stem: An application vendor disclosed a critical vulnerability in a library used by a customer-facing web application. The patch is available but requires a full application redeploy. Business operations require the application to be available 24/7. Which approach BEST balances security and availability?
pairs.option: Block all incoming traffic to the application until the vendor releases a hotfix that does not require a full redeploy

pairs.stem: A security architect is selecting a logging strategy for a regulated environment. Auditors require that logs be tamper-evident and retained for 7 years. Which approach BEST satisfies the requirement?
pairs.option: Encrypt logs at rest with a customer-managed key, restricting decryption to the audit team for after-the-fact review

pairs.stem: A penetration tester reports a finding to the security team: she discovered a path-traversal vulnerability in the company's customer portal that allows reading arbitrary files on the web server, including configuration files containing database credentials. What is the appropriate severity assessment under a CVSS-aligned framework?
pairs.option: High — the vulnerability discloses database credentials enabling lateral movement, even though it does not directly execute code

pairs.stem: A SOC analyst is investigating a series of failed login attempts against an executive's account. Logs show 12 failures over 4 hours from 7 different geographic locations, then a successful login from an 8th location. The user is on vacation in an entirely different country. Which response action should the analyst take FIRST?
pairs.option: Disable the account immediately, revoke active sessions, and escalate per incident-response playbook for suspected account compromise

pairs.stem: A new project is in the design phase. The architect is selecting between integrating security review as a separate phase before launch versus building security checks into each design and code-review iteration. Which approach is MOST aligned with secure SDLC best practice?
pairs.option: Integrate security review as a single gate immediately before production launch, since this provides a fresh look without iterative bias
